A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same WCMDP research, with matching authors, formulation, ID policy, and main theorem. Text and rendered pages support comparison of both complete documents, including their renumbered appendices.

before.justification: v3 presents algorithms, theoretical results, proofs, and related work. Neither its main text nor Appendices A–G report original empirical outcomes.

after.justification: Section 5 and Figures 1–2 report original WCMDP simulations, including comparison with ERC. Appendix B documents the simulated instances and baseline.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–2 retain their steps. However, v5 Remark 1 introduces an optional modification assigning arms with unbounded mixing times the largest IDs, effectively ignoring that fraction of arms.

E1.justification: v5 introduces empirical coverage absent from v3: randomly generated fully heterogeneous WCMDPs with four budget constraints, and ten-type heterogeneous problems with one budget constraint and costs depending only on actions (Section 5, Appendix B.1).

E2.justification: Figure 2 adds ERC from Xiong et al. [46] as an evaluated comparator. v3 discusses that work only as related research. The addition comprises one baseline evaluated under its restricted problem setting.

E3.justification: v5 establishes the first experimental protocols: six arm counts from 100 to 3200, ten states and four actions per arm, 20,000 simulation time steps, and an optimality-ratio metric normalized by the LP upper bound. The ERC comparison uses a compatible restricted setting.

E4.justification: Figure 1 adds a finite-size scaling analysis, varying the arm count to examine convergence toward the LP upper bound. v3 contains only theoretical analysis of this behavior. No component ablations or distribution-shift tests are added.

E5.justification: Section 5 newly reports four replications for each arm count and confidence intervals calculated using batch means with batch size 4000. v3 has no experimental uncertainty reporting; this is not an increase over previously reported runs.

E6.justification: v5 adds the first empirical results. Figure 1 shows the ID optimality ratio rising approximately from 0.90 at 100 arms to 0.98 at 3200 arms. Figure 2 shows ID exceeding ERC in the illustrated instance; the text reports comparable performance in other instances. v3 has no corresponding empirical results.

T1.justification: v5 adds Proposition 1's finite-time reward bound, C_ID/√N + C_finite/T, with a derivation in Appendix I and an intermediate bound in Appendix H.2. Remark 1 also extends the guarantee to a vanishing fraction of poorly mixing arms and remaining mixing times growing as o(N^(1/8)). The original main theorem and Assumption 1 remain.

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution paragraphs retain the same headline claims: an efficiently computable ID policy, the first asymptotic-optimality result for fully heterogeneous average-reward WCMDPs, and projection-based Lyapunov functions as the central innovation.

C2.justification: v5 expands the mechanism explanation by connecting cost convergence to budget slack and additional conforming arms. It also replaces strict-contraction wording with negative-drift language and qualifies the empirical advantage over ERC as instance-dependent.

D1.justification: New Appendix B specifies random instance-generation distributions, budget sampling, and the ERC implementation. It adds experimental code-access information and a reported reproduction time within 24 hours on a standard PC, exemplified by a six-core Intel Core i7.

R1.justification: Sections 1–2 and Appendix A expand the treatment of already-cited Hong et al. [25], acknowledging its fully heterogeneous FTVA extension and similar LP. They explain the synchronization-time condition and distinguish its restless-bandit scope from general WCMDPs. The broader literature framework is retained.

P1.justification: v5 makes localized prose revisions in the introduction, LP discussion, and related work, and standardizes budget-constraint terminology. It adds the experiments section and two appendices while preserving the existing narrative order and proof organization.

P2.justification: v5 adds two labeled line plots with legends and LP-reference lines, arranged beside the experimental discussion. Existing algorithm displays and the overall single-column format remain, with ordinary text and equation reflow.

improvement.justification: The finite-time derivation and mixing-time extension make the retained theoretical result more informative. Specified simulations, uncertainty reporting, code-access information, and clearer positioning against FTVA improve assessability and reproducibility. These are useful additions to a largely unchanged theoretical core, while the empirical evidence remains limited to two synthetic settings.
